title: Why Japan's $20 Billion Airport Is Sinking
sources: Landsat data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey

chapters.title: An Island That Was Not There

paragraphs.text: This is Osaka Bay in 1985. Open water. Ten years later there is an island here, three miles from the shore, with an airport on it. Japan built it from nothing. And it has been sinking ever since.

shots.photo: File:Kansai Airport terminal 1 ,from the top of observation hall "sky view" (16041786233).jpg

paragraphs.text: By the operator's own measurements, the ground under the first island has dropped almost fourteen meters since the fill began. That is forty-five feet, the height of a four-storey building. Last year it went down five centimeters more. Every one of those numbers comes from the company that runs the airport, which measures the island at seventeen points and publishes the result.

stat.label: Average settlement of the first island since construction began (45 ft)
stat.source: Kansai Airports, measurements of December 2025

stat.label: Settlement of the first island in 2025, average of 17 points
stat.source: Kansai Airports, measurements of December 2025

paragraphs.text: Then Japan built a second island beside it. That one is sinking four times as fast.

Thirty-four million passengers used this airport last year. So why did Japan build its airport in the sea, why did the forecasts miss, and how long can it last? We will watch every stage of it from orbit.

ask.text: Why build an airport in the sea?

paragraphs.text: Osaka already had an airport. Itami sits inland, north of the city, with houses on every side. The first jet landed there in 1964. Almost at once the neighbours began to protest and to sue over the noise, and in the end Japan's supreme court awarded them compensation.

Near Tokyo, the government had tried to build a new airport on farmland at Narita, and met years of protest from the people who lived there. Planners in Osaka did not want a second Narita. From 1968 the transport ministry studied two sites on land and six at sea.

Land near a big city is expensive, and so is paying thousands of neighbours for the noise. Building new land offshore can look cheaper in the long run. So they looked at the one place where nobody lived: the bay. In 1974 the choice was made: an island in the south of the bay, five kilometers out to sea, placed so that planes would arrive and leave entirely over water, around the clock. The airport's own engineers later called it a radical solution to the noise problems of Itami.

document.text: "Kansai International Airport was built five kilometers out to sea on Osaka Bay as a radical solution to the noise problems of Osaka (Itami) Airport."
document.source: S. Suzuki and Y. Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., in JSCE Civil Engineering, 2008
document.highlight: a radical solution to the noise problems

paragraphs.text: We had to decide to build offshore because there were few viable options, an urban planning professor, Hiro Ishikawa, told This Week in Asia last year. There was one problem with the site. There was no land there.

document.text: "We had to decide to build offshore because there were few viable options."
document.source: Hiro Ishikawa, emeritus professor, Meiji University, to This Week in Asia, 2025

paragraphs.text: The water at the site is about twenty meters deep. Under it lies about twenty meters of soft clay, and that clay is seventy percent water. Put weight on it and the water is squeezed out, the way it leaves a sponge. Engineers call it consolidation. This spot has been under water for ten thousand years. The operator expected the layer to shrink to two thirds of its thickness.

stat.label: Share of water in the soft clay under the bay, by volume
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: Left alone, that would take decades. So the builders gave the water a way out. They drove one million columns of sand into the clay, each twenty meters long, two and a half meters apart. Each began as a pipe pounded into the seabed, filled with sand and pulled out again, leaving the sand behind. Water cannot climb through clay, but it can creep sideways into the sand, and from there it rises and drains away. That was more than all of Japan had installed in the thirty-five years before. It worked: a process of decades was over within a year.

stat.label: Sand drains under the first island, 20 m long, 2.5 m apart
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: In 1987 they started a wall around an empty rectangle of sea, built of rubble and forty-eight thousand concrete blocks, anchored in steel chambers that weigh hundreds of tons. This is our own image from September 1989. The wall is finished. Inside it there is still water.

shots.photo: File:Kansai Airport terminal 1 ,from the top of observation hall "sky view" (16041786233).jpg

paragraphs.text: Then came the fill. A hundred and eighty million cubic meters of rock and soil, quarried at four sites ten to thirty kilometers away and carried out by barge. A year later, in our image from August 1990, the rectangle is half full and a bridge is reaching out from the shore. The plan was a layer thirty meters deep. As the forecasts of sinking grew, so did the layer, to almost thirty-seven. At times the heap stood sixty-five feet above the sea, waiting to settle.

stat.label: Height of the fill above the sea floor, first island: planned and final
stat.source: Mesri & Funk, J. Geotech. Geoenviron. Eng., ASCE, 2015

paragraphs.text: While the fill was still under water it was partly afloat, and the deep seabed hardly moved. The sinking began in earnest when the island rose above the surface and its full weight came down. The fill itself was packing down too, under its own load. The bridge, nearly four kilometers long, was finished. On September fourth, 1994, the airport opened.

But the sand drains reached only the soft top layer. Under it lies something older. For two million years the sea here rose and fell by more than a hundred meters as ice ages came and went, laying down clay, then sand, then clay again. When this was sea, clay settled on the bottom. When it was dry land or a lake shore, sand did. All the while the crust under the bay was slowly going down, so nothing washed away. The borings went down four hundred meters and found twenty-two layers of clay with sand between them, and its upper part is the softer part: under enough pressure it gives. Nobody can drain it, and squeezing the water out of clay like that takes anything from decades to hundreds of years. The operator's own page says the airport is managed on the assumption that long-term subsidence will continue.

stat.label: 22 clay layers (290 m in all) and 19 sand layers under the second island
stat.source: Mesri & Funk, J. Geotech. Geoenviron. Eng., ASCE, 2015

document.text: "...the airport facilities are managed with the assumption that long-term subsidence will continue."
document.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports (3)

paragraphs.text: The planners knew the island would sink, and they piled on enough soil to allow for it. The plan was that after fifty years the ground would still stand thirteen feet above the sea. That was not a comfort margin. It is the least height the island needs to stay dry if a wave breaks through the wall. By 1990, before a single building stood on it, the island had sunk twenty-seven feet instead of the nineteen predicted. An ordinary landfill on a coast is too light to bother clay that old. This one, built in deep water, was heavy enough to make it give.

shots.photo: File:Kansai Airport terminal 1 ,from the top of observation hall "sky view" (16041786233).jpg

chart.title: Sinking of the first island by 1990

paragraphs.text: The amount of soil was set by a fifty-year estimate of the sinking, a spokeswoman for the operator, Yukako Handa, told Air and Space magazine in 2018. The engineers, she said, simply could not believe the gap between their laboratory estimates and what the seabed really did. By opening day the ground had already gone down almost ten meters. Parts of the island reached the fifty-year limit within six years, and at least a hundred and fifty million dollars went into raising the seawall.

document.text: "...the amount of soil to reclaim the land was determined based on necessary ground level and subsidence estimation over 50 years after the construction."
document.source: Yukako Handa, Kansai Airports, to Air & Space / Smithsonian, June 2018

stat.label: Settlement of the first island before the airport opened in 1994
stat.source: Kansai Airports, measurements of December 2025

stat.label: Spent to raise the seawall as the island sank
stat.source: Air & Space / Smithsonian, June 2018

paragraphs.text: An island does not sink evenly. So the terminal, a mile long, stands on nine hundred columns, each with its own gauge. When one drops, it is jacked up and steel plates are slid underneath. The middle of the building has a basement, which makes it lighter than the wings, so the builders packed iron ore under it as ballast. It still sank less than its neighbours, and had to be levelled. The jacks are still worked every few years. The buildings sit on rafts of concrete, so that each one goes down as a whole, and soil was dug away around the heavy ones to keep the load on the ground even.

stat.label: Columns under Terminal 1, each monitored and jacked up when needed
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: The sinking reached things nobody had drawn. Rain was meant to run off the runway and out to sea through pipes, downhill. As the ground settled, the slope disappeared. The airport installed thirty-seven large pumps to push its own rainwater out, and in 2007 it covered the whole first runway with new asphalt, twenty-five centimeters thick on average, to give the water a slope again. The runways are asphalt for the same reason: asphalt bends where concrete would crack.

document.text: "...with the progression of uneven settlement... the angle of the drainage pipes has gradually lessened, hampering the flow of rainwater into the ocean."
document.source: S. Suzuki and Y. Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., in JSCE Civil Engineering, 2008
document.highlight: the angle of the drainage pipes has gradually lessened

stat.label: Installed at ten sites, 3,300 cubic meters a minute
stat.source: Suzuki & Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., JSCE, 2008

stat.label: Asphalt laid on Runway A in 2007-2008, 25 cm thick on average
stat.source: Kansai Airports

paragraphs.text: And yet the island held. In January 1995, four months after opening, the Kobe earthquake struck less than thirty kilometers away and killed more than six thousand people. By the accounts we found, the airport came through undamaged. In 2001 the American Society of Civil Engineers named it one of the civil engineering monuments of the millennium.

One runway was not enough. In 1999 work began on a second island, in deeper water. This time the builders drove one point two million sand drains. This is our image from 2004, with the new island still being filled. Its runway, four kilometers long, opened in August 2007. Together the two islands are a little over ten square kilometers of land that did not exist.

stat.label: Sand drains under the second island
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: The builders had learned. They laid the new ground in layers sixty centimeters thick and rolled each one. They built a test track and drove a vehicle as heavy as a jumbo jet around it fifteen thousand times. The ground held so well that the runway pavement could be half as thick as on the first island.

stat.label: Test runs with a vehicle as heavy as a jumbo jet on the second island
stat.source: Kansai Airports, Technologies for Offshore Airports

paragraphs.text: By the time that runway opened, the seabed under it had already gone down almost twelve meters. It has gone down six more since. In 2025 the second island sank twenty centimeters, four times as fast as the first, whose rate fell under ten centimeters a year long ago.

stat.label: Settlement under the second island: 11.71 m before 2007, 5.96 m since
stat.source: Kansai Airports, measurements of December 2025

paragraphs.text: An engineering professor at the University of Illinois, Gholamreza Mesri, has studied both islands for years. In a 2015 paper with his colleague Funk he forecast that by the end of this century the seabed under the first island will have settled about seventeen and a half meters, and under the second more than twenty-four. Left to itself, they wrote, the surface of the first island would be at sea level by 2067 or sooner. The operator makes no such promise. It says only that it will keep measuring, with the guidance of experts. In 2018 Mesri told Air and Space that the second island could come down to its warning height, thirteen feet above the sea, as early as 2023. Which is why the walls keep going up.

stat.label: Forecast settlement by the end of the century, first and second island
stat.source: Mesri & Funk, J. Geotech. Geoenviron. Eng., ASCE, 2015

chapters.title: The Sea Comes Over the Wall

paragraphs.text: A sinking island in a typhoon sea needs its walls to keep up. It stands in twenty meters of open water, where its engineers feared high tides more than tsunamis. In 2004 a run of typhoons brought the highest tides and waves the airport had recorded. Waves came over the seawall and destroyed a road behind it. So the company raised the walls, by one to two meters, along eleven kilometers of shore.

document.text: "Waves flowed over the airport's seawalls, destroying a road behind the seawall."
document.source: S. Suzuki and Y. Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., in JSCE Civil Engineering, 2008
document.highlight: destroying a road behind the seawall

stat.label: Seawalls raised along about 11 km after the 2004 typhoons
stat.source: Suzuki & Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., JSCE, 2008

paragraphs.text: The sea was also coming from below. The island is made of crushed rock, and the water inside it rose and fell with the tide, into basements. So between 2004 and 2006 the company built a wall underground, about thirty meters deep, all the way around the island. It lowered the water in the ground by a meter and a half. All of it was done beside a working runway, with machines kept under fifteen meters tall so that no aircraft could strike one. The pumps were sized for a cloudburst of fifty-five millimeters in an hour.

stat.label: Underground cut-off wall around the island, about 30 m deep, 2004-2006
stat.source: Suzuki & Okuda, Kansai International Airport Co., JSCE, 2008

paragraphs.text: Then came September fourth, 2018, twenty-four years to the day after the airport opened. Typhoon Jebi, reported as the strongest to hit Japan in twenty-five years, pushed the sea over the walls and across a runway. A tanker of about two thousand six hundred tons, the Houn Maru, dragged its anchor and hit the only bridge. By most reports about three thousand passengers were stuck on the island overnight, and left the next morning by boat. Flights began again within days. The bridge was not whole until the following spring.

stat.label: Passengers stranded overnight on 4 Sep 2018, by most press reports
stat.source: Press reports, Sep 2018

paragraphs.text: The walls went up again. Within three years, with planes still landing, the operator raised the seawalls along more than six kilometers, laid wave-breaking blocks along nearly five, and went on raising the first runway. Japan's society of civil engineers gave the work an award. The rule, in the operator's own brochure, is simple: as the island sinks, the walls are raised to the height the worst expected waves would need.

stat.label: Seawalls raised after Typhoon Jebi; blocks placed along 4.7 km
stat.source: Kansai Airports, via ACI Asia-Pacific, May 2022

paragraphs.text: None of this was cheap. When the airport opened, its cost was put at about eight billion dollars. By 2008, with the repairs, the second island and its runway, the figure was about twenty billion.

The airport carried that as debt, and for years it charged some of the highest landing fees in the world to pay the interest: about seven and a half thousand dollars for one Boeing 747, by one count three times the price at New York's JFK. In 2016 the state handed the running of the airport to a private group led by Orix of Japan and Vinci of France. Two years later that group was paying the transport ministry about three hundred and fifty million dollars a year for the right. Itami never closed. It still takes domestic flights, and the same company now runs both.

stat.label: Paid each year to Japan's transport ministry for operating rights (2018)
stat.source: Air & Space / Smithsonian, June 2018

paragraphs.text: And the passengers came. Twenty-six million in 2016. Thirty-four million in 2025, most of them from abroad. A fully loaded Airbus A380, the operator likes to point out, weighs less than three ten-thousandths of one percent of the soil it lands on.

chart.title: Passengers a year
chart.source: Air & Space, 2018; Kansai Airports traffic figures

paragraphs.text: The operator gives no official lifetime for the islands. Its spokeswoman said so in 2018: no such figure has been calculated. The first one now sinks a few centimeters a year, not half a meter. We knew from the start that the airport would subside, Professor Ishikawa said, and we considered the various impacts in the design. The settling may go on for centuries, only slower.

document.text: "We knew from the start that the airport would subside, and we considered the various impacts in the design."
document.source: Hiro Ishikawa, emeritus professor, Meiji University, to This Week in Asia, 2025

paragraphs.text: Japan kept building this way. Chubu, near Nagoya, in 2005. Kobe, across the bay, in 2006. Kitakyushu the same year. All of them on islands made in the sea. And not only Japan. When Air and Space looked in 2018, new runways were going up on a drained marsh north of Istanbul, on a reef in the Maldives and on river mud in Brisbane. Ground like that settles. The only question is how fast, and who is still measuring.
So here is the question. If your city had no room left for an airport, would you build one on the sea, knowing it would sink?

ask.text: Would you build it, knowing it would sink?

youtube.title: Why Japan's $20 Billion Airport Is Sinking
youtube.description: In 1985 this part of Osaka Bay was open water. Japan built an island there, opened Kansai International Airport on it in 1994, and the ground has dropped more than 13 meters since the fill began. From orbit with our own Landsat and Sentinel-2 images we watch the island appear, follow the second island that is sinking faster, and go through the forecasts that missed, the typhoon that cut the airport off in 2018, and what it costs to keep an airport above the sea.
youtube.pinned_comment: If your city had no room left for an airport, would you build one on the sea, knowing it would sink?
